food.text: The earliest known mention of "feijoada à brasileira" is an advertisement in the Diário de Pernambuco of March 2, 1827, in Recife. It said that the Locanda da Águia d'Ouro, on das Cruzes Street, would serve excellent Brazilian-style feijoada on Thursdays for a comfortable price.

In 1907, the government of São Paulo signed a contract to bring Japanese migrants to work in the city's new coffee business. The first wave arrived on the ship Kasato Maru and landed at the port of Santos. Their first meal on Brazilian soil was rice and beans, and the soft, non-sticky Brazilian rice was unlike what they knew in Japan.

Between 1882 and 1914, 1.5 million immigrants of different nationalities came to São Paulo, and 695,000 of them left the state, or 45% of the total. Many left after their experience on São Paulo's coffee farms, where Italians lived in semi-slavery conditions: they were monitored, made to work long hours, sometimes forced to buy what they needed from the landowner, and replaced if they refused the landowners' terms. An estimated 223,031 Italians left Brazil between 1890 and 1904, mainly after failed experiences on the coffee farms.

On January 6, 1849, the Jornal do Commercio of Rio de Janeiro announced that the newly installed Novo Café do Commércio restaurant would serve "A Bella Feijoada à Brazilleira" every Tuesday and Thursday, at the request of many customers. Years earlier, in 1833, Recife's newly opened Hôtel Théatre had advertised the dish on Thursdays.

Immigrants from Lebanon began arriving in Brazil in the late 19th century. Their cooking left a lasting mark, and dishes such as sfiha, hummus, kibbeh, tahina, tabbouleh and halwa are now very well known among Brazilians.

On March 3, 1840, Father Carapuceiro wrote in the Diário de Pernambuco that in families ignorant of true gastronomy, the previous day's dinner leftovers were turned into feijoada, which they called "the burial of the bones". Turkey, suckling pig, bacon, ham and dried meat known as ceará all went into one pot with the indispensable beans.

In 1860, Oscar Comettant described feijoada as salted, sun-dried meat, small black beans, bacon and very coarse cassava flour, mixed into a dark porridge that looks unappealing but tastes very pleasant. He called it the important dish of every modest dinner in Brazil, comparing it to the French pot-au-feu and the puchero in Spain.

Japanese immigrants at first ate rice and cod, but they did not know how to desalt cod and prepared it over hot coals. Because rice was expensive, it was replaced by cookies made of cornmeal, cassava flour and corn, eaten to complement the morning coffee.

The Rio de Janeiro restaurant G. Lobo, at 135 General Câmara Street, was very popular for its feijoada completa, served with rice, sliced oranges, sautéed kale and farofa. Founded at the end of the 19th century, it disappeared in 1905 when Uruguaiana Street was widened.

Preserves, which are fundamental to Japanese cuisine, did not exist in Brazil at that time, so the immigrants pickled local fruits like papaya. Familiar items such as fish and vegetables were also hard to find at first, because they were not part of the local diet.

art.text: Brazilian academic art grew out of the Royal School of Sciences, Arts and Crafts, founded by John VI in 1816 and encouraged by the French Artistic Mission. It flourished under the Imperial Academy of Fine Arts and the patronage of Dom Pedro II. The system lasted into the early 20th century.
tags: Royal School of Sciences, Arts and Crafts

art.text: In the middle of the Amazon rainforest, wealthy rubber barons tried to recreate the lavish lifestyle of European elites by building the Teatro Amazonas opera house in Manaus. Construction began in 1884 under the supervision of an Italian architect.

In 1879 a Salon in Rio de Janeiro became a landmark for the popularization of academic art. It featured The Battle of Avaí by Pedro Américo and The Battle of Guararapes by Victor Meirelles. The public success was overwhelming, attracting virtually the entire population of Rio and sparking a debate about art that lasted for months.

The Teatro Amazonas was assembled from materials gathered from across the world. Its roofing came from Alsace, its furniture from Paris, its marble from Italy and its steel from England. The dome is covered with 36,000 decorated ceramic tiles painted in the colors of the Brazilian flag: blue, yellow and green.

The French Artistic Mission arrived in Brazil in 1816 and helped spread neoclassical ideals from Rio, which needed a reorganized urban plan after the Portuguese royal family arrived. Its architect, Grandjean de Montigny, became Professor of Architecture at the Royal School of Sciences, Arts and Crafts.
tags: Royal School of Sciences, Arts and Crafts

art.text: Between 1870 and 1880, works of art circulated more widely among the nobility and wealthy bourgeoisie. This was driven by depoliticized themes such as landscapes, genre scenes, portraits and still lifes. The first commercial art gallery opened in Rio in 1875, and critics such as Gonzaga Duque helped educate the public through magazines and newspapers.

When the Portuguese Court moved to Brazil in 1808, fleeing the French invasion of Portugal, King John VI brought part of the Portuguese Royal Collection to Rio de Janeiro. After he returned to Europe, much of it stayed in Brazil and became the core of European art in what is now the Museu Nacional de Belas Artes.

Grandjean de Montigny designed the Comércio Square in Rio, built between 1819 and 1820, a building with a grandiose dome and centered plan. Although he built little of what he designed, his architectural classes trained several architects who helped establish the neoclassical style throughout the Empire period.

Academy graduates struggled to build careers because the main consumer market for academic art was the State and the imperial family. Some draftsmen found jobs with the Army, some engravers at the Mint, and architects in the Public Works Department. Many others had to adopt other professions.

Joachim Lebreton, a French artist, led the French Artistic Mission that came to Brazil in 1816 to help organise the arts in the country. He enlarged the royal collection with paintings he brought with him. The mission's aim was to set up the country's first art academy.

Grandjean designed the main building of the Royal School, inaugurated only in 1826 and considered a pure expression of French neoclassicism. It had a symmetrical façade and a great centralized portal in Ionic order. That portal is the only element to survive, installed in the Botanical Garden of Rio de Janeiro.
tags: Royal School of Sciences, Arts and Crafts
Botanical Garden of Rio de Janeiro

war.text: The Battle of Acosta Ñu on 16 August 1869 was the last major engagement of the Paraguayan War. About 3,500 poorly armed Paraguayans, mostly boys between nine and fifteen years old, old men and wounded combatants, confronted 20,000 Brazilian and Argentine veteran soldiers. Paraguayans remember it as the Children's Battle, and mark 16 August as Children's Day to commemorate the children who lost their lives in it.

The Cisplatine War was fought in the 1820s between the Empire of Brazil and the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata over control of the Banda Oriental, which Brazil had annexed as the province of Cisplatina. The war resulted in the independence of Cisplatina as the Oriental State of Uruguay.
tags: United Provinces of the Río de la Plata

war.text: Brazil's war of independence was fought across Bahia, Maranhão, Pará, Piauí and Cisplatina, with naval battles along the Atlantic coast. Fights between Portuguese soldiers and local militias broke out in the streets of the main cities in 1822 and spread inland, and the Brazilian side filled its ranks by forced enlistment of citizens, foreign immigrants and mercenaries, and by enlisting slaves who were promised freedom for military service. Brazilian troops numbered between 30,000 and 40,000 men against around 20,000 Portuguese, and the siege of Salvador ended with the surrender of approximately 10,000 Portuguese troops on 2 July 1823. The victory established the Empire of Brazil under emperor Pedro I.

After the republic was created in 1889, the regime had to subdue many rebellions. They included the Two Naval Revolts (1891 and 1893–94), the Federalist Rebellion (1893–95) and the War of Canudos (1896–97). The Contestado War, which pitted settlers against landowners, raged from 1912 to 1916.

The Duke of Caxias, commander of the allied forces, suggested in 1869 that the Paraguayan War was militarily over. Emperor Pedro II refused to stop until Francisco Solano López surrendered, so Caxias resigned. He was replaced by the Emperor's son-in-law, Prince Gaston of Orleans, the Count of Eu.

The Paraguayan commander Bernardino Caballero disguised many of the nine- and ten-year-olds in his ranks with false beards, to hide how young most of his forces were. They faced some 20,000 Brazilian and Argentine soldiers at Acosta Ñu, and the article says the children were among those who lost their lives in the battle.

In 1825 a group of patriots known as the Thirty-Three Orientals, led by Juan Antonio Lavalleja, rebelled against Brazil. On 25 August they declared Cisplatina's independence at the Congress of Florida. After initial skirmishes they defeated the Brazilians at the battles of Rincón and Sarandí.

In 1889 a coup d'état led by Deodoro da Fonseca deposed Emperor Pedro II and began the First Brazilian Republic. Its first period, the Republic of the Sword (1889-1894), was a military dictatorship under Marshals Deodoro da Fonseca and Floriano Peixoto.

By 1864 the Brazilian army had been so neglected that it had only 18,000 men and lacked equipment, ammunition, uniforms and transportation. The National Guard was enrolled at 440,000, but most of its members resisted being sent to the front and had little training or equipment. The Fatherland Volunteer Corps, created on 7 January 1865 to take both volunteers and conscripts, helped raise the force in enemy territory to 82,271 men by 1869. The Paraguayan War lasted more than five years and cost the lives of 50,000 Brazilians.
war.source_title: Military of the Empire of Brazil

war.text: The battle began at 8:30 in the morning on Campo Grande, an open plain of about 12 square kilometres that favored the Brazilian cavalry. Because two streams narrowed the approach to the field, the Allied 1st Infantry Corps under Col. Manoel Deodoro da Fonseca led the initial attack.

After the victories at Rincón and Sarandí, the Argentine Congress proclaimed Cisplatina reintegrated into the United Provinces on 25 October 1825. In response, Brazil declared war on the United Provinces on 10 December 1825 and imposed a naval blockade on the River Plate.
tags: United Provinces of the Río de la Plata

war.text: Fires spread through the dry grass of the Acosta Ñu battlefield, and many injured soldiers died in them. Historian Julio José Chiavenatto accused the Count of Eu of ordering fires set to kill fallen soldiers, including burning a field hospital. The Viscount of Taunay, who was present, blamed the Paraguayans for setting fires to hide their movements, which then spread out of control.

When war broke out in December 1825, Brazil's naval forces in the River Plate included the frigate Tétis, the corvette Liberal, 2 brigs, a barque, 12 schooners and 8 gunboats. The same fleet, under Pedro Nunes, had fought the Portuguese in Brazil's independence war and Artigas in 1820.

literature.text: Brazilian literature long followed the literary trends of Portugal. Over the 19th and 20th centuries it gradually shifted toward an authentic writing style, searching for truly Brazilian themes and forms.

Joaquim Maria Machado de Assis (1839 to 1908) is usually named the greatest Brazilian writer of all time and the most important writer of Brazilian Realism. Born in Rio de Janeiro, he was the natural son of a half-black wallpainter and a Portuguese woman. His only education, besides literacy classes, was extensive reading of borrowed books.

Afro-Brazilian literature in written form began in the mid-19th century with Maria Firmina dos Reis's novel Ursula in 1859. Other writers of the late 19th century include Machado de Assis and Cruz e Sousa. Oral traditions, however, can be traced back to the 16th century, when African slaves were brought across the Atlantic.

The gaucho epic poem Martin Fierro by Argentine José Hernández is among the iconic and populist 19th-century literary works written in Spanish and published in Latin America. Alberto Blest Gana's Martin Rivas, an adventure novel about the Chilean gold rush of the 1850s, belongs to the same group.

Neoclassicism lasted an unnaturally long time in Brazil, stifling innovation. It was only in 1836 that Romanticism began influencing Brazilian poetry on a large scale, principally through the efforts of the expatriate poet Gonçalves de Magalhães.

Maria Firmina dos Reis was born in São Luiz do Maranhão on October 11, 1825. Her 1859 book Úrsula approaches slavery from the perspective of the "Other". Because of attitudes silencing women, she signed it with the pseudonym "Uma Maranhense" (A Maranhese woman).

The novel Bom-Crioulo, written by Adolfo Caminha in 1895, is traditionally seen as the initiator of Brazilian LGBTQ literature. It is also considered the first LGBTQ novel in Latin America. Although Caminha shared a negative view of homosexuality, he was the first to center a plot on a same-sex relationship.

Brazilian science fiction emerged in the latter half of the 19th century, roughly parallel with the rising popularity of Jules Verne's work in France. Writers used motifs such as imaginary societies studied with scientific rigor and futuristic voyages, often set in the landscape of 19th century Brazil.

Around 1850, a Romantic transition centered on Álvares de Azevedo. His short story collection Noite na Taverna (A Night at the Tavern) and his poetry, collected after his death in Lira dos Vinte Anos (Twenty-year-old Lyre), became influential. He drew on Lord Byron and Alfred de Musset, and this second Romantic generation was obsessed with morbidity and death.

Euclides da Cunha, who was tormented by family problems and was killed by his wife's lover, covered the Canudos War (1895-97), a popular revolt in Bahia, as a journalist. His trilogy Os Sertões is composed of three parts titled "The Land", "The Man" and "The fight". This structure reinforces determinism, the idea that the environment where a man was born, his social surroundings and his culture define what he will become, a way of thought that deeply influenced Brazilian literature.

Many 19th-century white Brazilian writers wrote about Afro-Brazilians. Abolitionists among them included Castro Alves and Joaquim Nabuco, while Naturalist writers included Aluísio Azevedo, Jose Veríssimo and Raul Pompéia.
Machado de Assis published the short story O Imortal in 1882, and Emília Freitas published A Rainha do Ignoto in 1899. Both are counted among the notable early works of Brazilian science fiction.

Maria Firmina dos Reis was not revealed as the author of Úrsula until 1975. That year Horácio de Almeida published a facsimile of the book, more than a century after its 1859 publication under a pseudonym.

Between January and October 1907, the children's magazine O Tico-Tico published Viagens maravilhosas do Dr. Alpha ao mundo dos planetas. Written and illustrated by Oswaldo Silva, it is possibly the first space travel story in Brazilian literature.

science.text: Between 1808 and 1810, the government of D. João VI founded the Royal Naval Academy, the Royal Military Academy, the Biblioteca Nacional and the Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden. He gave impetus to bringing such European institutions to Brazil. All of this happened in a remarkably short period.

Emperor D. Pedro II came to the throne in 1841, when he was 15 years old. For the next 50 years Brazil enjoyed a stable constitutional monarchy. He was an enlightened monarch who favored the arts, literature, science and technology.
The mainstay of Brazilian science, and the seat of its first research laboratories, was the National Museum in Rio de Janeiro. The museum is still in existence today.

D. Pedro II developed a strong personal interest in science and invited many European scientific personalities, such as von Ihering and Goeldi, to work in Brazil. He and his ministers, courtesans and senators often attended scientific conferences at the National Museum.

The Medico-Chirurgical School of Bahia, founded under D. João VI between 1808 and 1810, is now known as the Faculdade de Medicina of the Universidade Federal da Bahia. The Medico-Chirurgical School of Rio de Janeiro became the Faculdade de Medicina of the Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro.
tags: Medico-Chirurgical School of Rio de Janeiro

science.text: The first laboratory of physiology in Brazil was founded at the National Museum in 1880. It was set up under João Baptista de Lacerda and Louis Couty.
Research universities and institutes were created in Brazil only at the beginning of the 20th century. The source calls this a long delay for education, science and technology in the country.

politics.text: On 7 September 1822, Prince Pedro declared the independence of Brazil and, after a successful war against his father's kingdom, was acclaimed on 12 October as Pedro I, the first Emperor of Brazil. The new country was huge, sparsely populated, and ethnically diverse.

In 1808, the Portuguese Prince regent, later King Dom John VI, fled Napoleon's invasion of Portugal and established his government in Rio de Janeiro. Brazil, a colony of the Kingdom of Portugal, thus became the seat of the Portuguese Empire.

On 13 May 1888, Princess Isabel signed the Golden Law, abolishing slavery once and for all and freeing the last 720,000 slaves in the country, about 5% of the population. Brazil was among the last countries in the Americas to abolish slavery.

Unlike most neighboring Hispanic American republics, the Empire of Brazil had political stability, vibrant economic growth and constitutionally guaranteed freedom of speech. There were legal restrictions on women and slaves, the latter regarded as property and not citizens.

In 1823, Pedro I convened a Constituent Assembly, but amid great disagreements with the parliamentarians it was dissolved in the Night of Agony. Some deputies had shouted for Pedro I to be declared an "outlaw" after he ordered the army to prepare for conflict. Deputies who had declared themselves ready to fall to the imperial bayonets went home unmolested, but six were deported to France, including the three Andradas. He then had a Council of State draft Brazil's first constitution, enacted the following year, which included the controversial moderating power.

Pedro I abdicated on 7 April 1831 in favor of his 5-year-old son, Pedro de Alcântara. The nobility and the army had both withdrawn their support, and his popularity had collapsed after the Cisplatine War's outcome and the murder of the journalist Líbero Badaró in São Paulo in 1830, carried out by police officers linked to the Empire. Pedro I was blamed for the death, and protests against him were violently repressed.

The 1823 draft constitution proposed that only free men in Brazil would count as Brazilian citizens, not slaves who might be freed. The promulgated 1824 document differed on this point. The draft also had far more restrictive electoral qualifications than the final text.

In 1828 the war in the south ended with the loss of Cisplatina, which became the independent republic of Uruguay. In the same year Prince Miguel usurped the throne of Maria II, Pedro I's daughter, worsening the emperor's position.
politics.source_title: History of the Empire of Brazil

politics.text: On 28 September 1885, under pressure, the Sexagenarian Law was enacted, guaranteeing freedom to slaves aged 60 or over, with slave owners receiving compensation. It regulated the gradual extinction of the servile element and preceded the Golden Law by less than three years.

A bill approved on June 12, 1823 stated that laws created by the Constituent Assembly would not need the Emperor's sanction. This, along with proposals to make the monarch a symbol completely subordinate to the Assembly, led Pedro I to confront the Assembly.

philosophy.text: In 1891, Brazil's first Republican Constitution ended the country's official religion, and Brazil has remained secular ever since. The Catholic Church nonetheless stayed politically influential into the 1970s. The constitution guarantees freedom of religion and bans government support or hindrance of religion.

Comtean Positivism was relatively popular in Brazil. In 1881, Miguel Lemos and Raimundo Teixeira Mendes organized the Positivist Church of Brazil after talks in Paris with Pierre Laffitte, a disciple of Auguste Comte who managed his estate. It grew out of Comte's secular Religion of Humanity.

In the 19th century most Brazilians were nominal Catholics, the nation was underserved by priests, and for large numbers of people religion did not play an important role in daily life. Protestantism largely originated with European immigrants and British American missionaries, following up on efforts that began in the 1820s.

After independence, Brazil's first constitution introduced freedom of religion in 1824 but kept Catholicism as the official religion. The Imperial government paid salaries to Catholic priests and influenced the appointment of bishops.

During Ramadan in January 1835, a small group of Black slaves and freedmen from Salvador da Bahia, inspired by Muslim teachers, rose up against the government in the Malê Revolt. It was the largest slave rebellion in Brazil. Muslims were called malê in Bahia at that time, and Scholars note that Brazil received more enslaved Muslims than anywhere else in the Americas.
Brazilian Positivists, religious or not, greatly influenced the republicanist movement. They were influential in the abolishment of the monarchy and the Proclamation of the Republic in 1889.

In 1871 in Recife, José Soriano de Souza published Lições de Filosofía Elementar, Racional e Moral, probably the earliest appearance of Neo-Thomism in Brazil. It came eight years before the Aeterni Patris encyclical. Its author was a lay physician who had studied philosophy at Leuven, but the book had no lasting influence.

After the Malê Revolt, fearing the example might be followed, Brazilian authorities began to watch the malês very carefully. In the following years they made intensive efforts towards conversions to Catholic Christianity and to erase the popular memory of and affection towards Islam. The African Muslim community was not erased overnight, though, and as late as 1910 an estimated 100,000 African Muslims were still living in Brazil.

In 1897 the Temple of Humanity was created in Brazil. Its services could go on for up to four hours, and combined with a certain moral strictness, this led to some decline during the Republican period.

Protestant missionaries in Brazil largely reached a working-class audience, since the upper class was wedded to Catholicism or secularism. By 1914, Protestant churches founded by U.S. missionaries had 47,000 communicants, served by 282 missionaries. They were more successful than in Mexico or Argentina.

The Positivist church appealed to the military class. Benjamin Constant joined the group but broke with it because he deemed Mendes and Lemos too fanatical. Cândido Rondon's conversion proved more solid: he remained an orthodox Positivist long after the church's importance waned.

culture.text: Batuques were drumming ceremonies that drew large crowds of enslaved Africans on Sunday evenings and holidays. Laws introduced in 1822 allowed police to shut them down, and the police repressed them. The gatherings persisted covertly on the town's outskirts or along the shoreline. In 1891 Adèle Toussaint-Samson wrote that the dancers went on at night, at the risk of being cruelly beaten.

In the 19th century, European cultural identity was the most valued in Brazil, while Afro-Brazilian culture was often neglected, discouraged and even prohibited. Afro-Brazilian religions and capoeira were often suppressed by the authorities, though congadas, maracatu and lundu were tolerated and even stimulated.

In the 19th century, most Brazilians were nominal Catholics, but the nation was underserved by priests, and for many people religion played no important role in daily life. Protestant missionaries mostly reached a working-class audience, since the upper class was wedded to Catholicism or secularism. By 1914, U.S.-founded Protestant churches had 47,000 communicants.

In 1891, the first Republican Constitution ended Brazil's official religion and made all religions equal in law. The Catholic Church nonetheless stayed very influential until the 1970s, and divorce was not allowed in Brazil until 1977.

In Bahia, the batuque dance evolved into various forms of samba, while the combat game practiced in the batuque circles was gradually absorbed by capoeira. In the province of Rio Grande, batuque became the general term for Afro-Brazilian religion.

The first Anglican chapel began offering services to English-speaking people in Rio de Janeiro in 1822. In 1827, the Prussian consul sponsored a German and French Reformed congregation in the same city, which today is a Lutheran church.

Hermann Blumenau arrived in southern Brazil in 1846, and in 1850 he returned from Germany with 17 pioneers to found a colony. By 1880 the colony became the municipality of Blumenau, with 15,000 inhabitants, mostly Germans, Austrians and Italians.

In the suburbs of Rio, batuque dances drew up to two thousand Africans, who danced in separate circles based on their nations. Many zungu houses organized these communal dances, where distinct nations also came together for common dances such as batuque, lundu, and capoeira.

Protestant missionaries in Brazil promoted schools, colleges and seminaries, including Mackenzie Presbyterian University in São Paulo. The Presbyterian schools in particular later became the nucleus of the governmental school system.

The Colônia Dona Francisca, today Joinville, was founded in 1851 on land that was part of the marriage dowry between Princess Francisca of Brazil and François d'Orléans, Prince of Joinville. Until 1888 it received 17,000 German-speaking immigrants, most of them Lutherans and farmers.
Africans devised tactics to protect the batuques from police. They would scatter when the police approached and reconvene elsewhere, and in some cases they answered police repression with violence.
